title: Armilla Launches Affirmative AI Liability Insurance with Lloyd's Underwriter, Chaucer
pub: PR Newswire (Cision) — press release issued by Armilla AI Inc., Toronto
author: Armilla AI Inc.

dom.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: Armilla supports the cluster’s account that AI coverage depends on policy wording and that conventional policies may leave material gaps. Its dedicated Lloyd’s-backed product illustrates specialist risk transfer, but the press release does not establish comprehensive coverage, claims performance, pricing adequacy or that insurance can substitute for governance and legal duties.
qs: There's a growing concern of 'silent AI cover' – the uncertainty of whether existing policies will respond to AI-specific failures, potentially mirroring the early, costly lessons of cyber risk," said Karthik Ramakrishnan, CEO of Armilla.
Tech E&O policies often lack sufficient limits, place the ensuing liabilities on the user, and do not extend to customized models.

mo.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Malpractice insurance: Reported AI claims remain hard to isolate

kp.k: Armilla launches affirmative insurance for AI failures
kp.d: Armilla announces an AI Liability Insurance policy, underwritten by certain Lloyd’s underwriters including Chaucer. The product is presented as affirmative AI-specific coverage intended to reduce uncertainty over whether conventional insurance responds to AI failures.
qs: Armilla Insurance Services (Armilla), Coverholder at Lloyd's, today announced the launch of its AI Liability Insurance policy.
Underwritten by certain underwriters at Lloyd's, including Chaucer, this pioneering policy provides affirmative coverage for AI.

kp.k: Silent AI coverage creates uncertainty for adopters
kp.d: Armilla CEO Karthik Ramakrishnan argues that insurance and risk-management tools have not kept pace with business adoption of AI. He characterizes “silent AI cover”—uncertainty about whether existing policies cover AI-specific failures—as a growing concern analogous to early cyber-insurance uncertainty.
qs: Businesses are racing to deploy AI, but their risk management and insurance tools haven't kept pace.
There's a growing concern of 'silent AI cover' – the uncertainty of whether existing policies will respond to AI-specific failures, potentially mirroring the early, costly lessons of cyber risk

kp.k: AI incidents reportedly generated over 150 US lawsuits
kp.d: As evidence of emerging legal exposure, the release states that AI incidents generated more than 150 US lawsuits during the preceding five years, attributing the figure to George Washington University researchers. It also asserts, without further quantified evidence, that AI regulation and scrutiny are increasing.
qs: As AI adoption continues to surge, AI incidents have spurred over 150 lawsuits in the US in the last 5 years per researchers at George Washington University.
AI regulations are proliferating and scrutiny intensifying, it's essential for AI adopters to protect themselves—regardless of fault.

kp.k: Traditional policies allegedly leave AI coverage gaps
kp.d: Armilla claims that technology errors-and-omissions policies may provide insufficient limits, allocate resulting liabilities to AI users, and exclude customized models. It further says enterprises without blanket E&O coverage face uncertainty for internally developed AI because of legacy wording, possible disputes, and future exclusions.
qs: Traditional insurance policies fall short on AI.
Tech E&O policies often lack sufficient limits, place the ensuing liabilities on the user, and do not extend to customized models.
Meanwhile, many enterprises lack blanket E&O coverage, leaving their internally developed AI solutions vulnerable to ambiguous legacy policy wording, potential disputes, and future exclusions.

kp.k: Coverage trigger focuses on AI application underperformance
kp.d: The policy is described as using a broad affirmative trigger based on AI applications underperforming, including failing to perform as intended or producing critical errors, hallucinations, or inaccuracies that cause damages. In this insurance context, “hallucinations” are treated as one category of potentially covered AI failure rather than as a measured model error rate.
qs: Armilla's AI Liability Insurance addresses key AI-related exposures by innovating a novel, broadly affirmative trigger around the risk of the underperformance of AI applications, such as the failure of the AI solution to perform as intended, generate critical errors, hallucinations or inaccuracies leading to damages.

kp.k: Policy covers legal costs and AI-failure liabilities
kp.d: Armilla states that the policy responds to covered AI failures by paying associated legal costs and liabilities. This positions AI malfunction as an insurable source of litigation and liability expense for organizations deploying AI, although the release does not provide policy language, exclusions, pricing, claim examples, or adjudicated coverage outcomes.
qs: Armilla's policy responses by covering legal costs and liabilities caused by AI failures.

kp.k: Chaucer says existing frameworks leave businesses exposed
kp.d: Nasra Ahmed of Chaucer endorses the product’s rationale, asserting that proliferating AI technologies create new challenges and that existing insurance frameworks often leave businesses exposed. She says the partnership combines Armilla’s technical insight with coverage intended to provide greater clarity and certainty for AI adopters.
qs: The proliferation of AI technology creates novel challenges that demand innovative insurance solutions
Existing frameworks often leave businesses exposed.

We are proud to partner with Armilla, leveraging their distinct technical insight to provide the market with a product that offers much-needed clarity and certainty for companies navigating the complexities of AI adoption.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Armilla claims that AI adoption creates insurance gaps and liability exposures that conventional policies do not adequately address.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about AI liability insurance, not a prediction about legal-service delivery. Armilla CEO Karthik Ramakrishnan says risk management and insurance have lagged AI deployment, creating uncertainty over whether existing policies cover AI-specific failures. The release claims that tech errors-and-omissions (E&O) policies often have insufficient limits, place ensuing liabilities on users and do not cover customized models. It also claims that enterprises without blanket E&O coverage face ambiguous wording, disputes and potential future exclusions for internally developed AI. Chaucer Senior Innovation Manager Nasra Ahmed similarly describes AI as creating novel insurance challenges. The comparison to early cyber-risk experience is a warning about a possible parallel, not a reported outcome.

pts.k: Armilla presents AI litigation and expanding regulation as reasons for adopters to obtain protection.
pts.d: The release states that AI incidents have generated more than 150 US lawsuits over the preceding five years, attributing that figure to George Washington University researchers. It also asserts that AI regulations and scrutiny are increasing, and argues that adopters need protection regardless of fault. This is a claim about exposure and the need for insurance, not a finding that adopters are legally liable regardless of fault.

pts.k: Armilla claims its newly launched policy explicitly covers AI failure-related legal costs and liabilities, supporting more confident AI deployment.
pts.d: Armilla announces affirmative AI liability coverage underwritten by certain Lloyd's underwriters, including Chaucer. It describes a broad coverage trigger based on AI underperformance, including failure to perform as intended and errors, hallucinations or inaccuracies leading to damages. Ramakrishnan claims this gives businesses confidence to innovate responsibly; Ahmed says the partnership offers clarity and certainty for AI adopters. These are product descriptions and anticipated benefits, rather than reported claims-payment or adoption outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The release offers one attributed litigation count; its other claims rest on company assertions and statements from participating executives.
pts.d: The quantitative basis is the claim of over 150 US lawsuits in five years, attributed to George Washington University researchers without identifying a study, methodology or individual cases. Claims about conventional policy gaps, regulatory proliferation and improved deployment confidence are not accompanied by supporting datasets or comparative analyses. The product's launch and coverage are described by Armilla and its underwriting partner; the text links to a coverage webpage but does not reproduce policy wording, exclusions, numerical limits or claims-payment experience.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern conditions at the April 30, 2025 launch, with a retrospective five-year litigation count and undated prospective benefits.
pts.d: The policy is announced as launching on April 30, 2025. The litigation statistic covers the preceding five years, without exact start and end dates. Coverage gaps and regulatory scrutiny are presented as current conditions; future exclusions and a possible repetition of early cyber-risk problems are prospective risks. The described policy response concerns AI failures causing liabilities or legal costs, with the trigger discussion referring to underperformance leading to damages. The release provides no detailed coverage qualifications or timetable for the claimed benefits to innovation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified affected groups are business AI adopters and developers, users facing liability, and insurers adapting their products.
pts.d: Armilla identifies businesses deploying AI, enterprises developing internal AI and users of customized models as exposed to uncertain or inadequate conventional coverage. Its proposed benefit is explicit insurance for AI-related legal costs and liabilities, alongside increased deployment confidence. Armilla, Chaucer and participating Lloyd's underwriters occupy the insurance-provider side of this response. The release does not identify particular legal-profession roles, law-firm segments or access-to-justice beneficiaries.
